evidence: Wikipedia's articles on 'Blue Monday' and New Order: released by Factory as FAC 73 on 7 March 1983, in a die-cut sleeve by Peter Saville that cost so much Factory lost money on each copy sold; it became the best-selling 12-inch single, with UK sales of 1.16 million across formats. New Order and Factory also financed the Haçienda club, opened in May 1982, which lost both a great deal of money.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen to 'Blue Monday' as a label decision as much as a song: seven and a half minutes, released only as a 12-inch for clubs, with no band photo and no title on the sleeve. That was Factory's way of doing things. It sold over a million copies and lost the label money on every one.

explanation: Factory Records released 'Blue Monday' in 1983 in an expensive sleeve designed to look like a computer floppy disk. It became the best-selling 12-inch single ever, but the sleeve cost so much that Factory lost money on every copy. It is the clearest case on the map of a label's values beating its accounts: design and freedom first, money later or never. The Haçienda club, paid for by the same label and band, is the same story the size of a building.
